title: Night Game Drives in Kenya: Where They Are Allowed, What You See and Cost
meta_title: Night Game Drives in Kenya: 6 Top Spots and Costs
meta_description: Night game drives in Kenya: where they are allowed (Mara conservancies, Ol Pejeta, Laikipia), what you see, costs and tips. Plan yours today.
excerpt: Night game drives in Kenya are allowed in private conservancies, not most national parks. Here is where to go, what you will see and what it costs.
content:
Night game drives in Kenya are allowed in private and community conservancies, not in most national parks or the Masai Mara National Reserve. The best places are the Mara conservancies, Laikipia (including Ol Pejeta) and other private reserves, where a guide and spotter search with a filtered spotlight for leopards, hyenas, aardvarks and other nocturnal animals.

Many travellers only discover after booking that their lodge sits in a park where driving stops at dusk. This guide explains where night game drives in Kenya are permitted, what you are likely to see, what they cost and how to build one into your itinerary so you do not miss the busiest hours of the African bush.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Quick Facts

  • Where allowed: Private and community conservancies (Mara, Laikipia, Ol Pejeta) and some private reserves
  • Where not allowed: Inside the Masai Mara National Reserve and as a routine activity in KWS national parks
  • Typical length: About 2 hours, usually starting after dinner or straight after sunset
  • Sample price: USD 70 per adult at Ol Pejeta (2026 tariff, checked October 2026)
  • Key sightings: Leopard, lion, hyena, aardvark, genet, bushbaby, porcupine, owls
  • Best season: Dry seasons (late June-October and January-February) for clearer tracks and denser game

Where Are Night Game Drives in Kenya Allowed?

Night game drives in Kenya are allowed on privately run land: Masai Mara conservancies, Laikipia ranches and conservancies such as Ol Pejeta, and some private sanctuaries. These areas set their own rules, cap vehicle numbers and permit spotlighting, off-road tracking and guided walks that the public parks and the reserve do not.

The split exists because national parks and national reserves are managed by public authorities with standard opening hours, while conservancies are managed with landowners and partner camps. That flexibility is the main reason many safari planners now pair a few nights in a national park with two or three nights in a conservancy.

AreaNight drives?Notes
Masai Mara National ReserveNoVehicles return to camp or leave the reserve by dusk
Mara conservancies (Naboisho, Mara North, Olare Motorogi, Ol Kinyei)YesRun by conservancy camps for their own guests
Ol Pejeta Conservancy (Laikipia)YesDaily slots 7pm-9pm and 9pm-11pm, booked a day ahead
Other Laikipia conservanciesYes, at many campsOften included in the camp rate
KWS national parks (Amboseli, Tsavo, Nairobi, Nakuru)Not as a routine activityVisitors leave by about 6pm unless camping inside; any exception is by special arrangement

Why can you not do night game drives in Kenya national parks?

Kenya's national parks are run by Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS), which asks day visitors to leave by about 6pm unless they are camping inside the park. The aim is to reduce poaching risk, protect wildlife from disturbance and keep visitors safe. A small number of lodges arrange night activities with special approval, but you should never assume one is available.

If night game drives in Kenya are a must for you, the simplest fix is to plan at least one stay in a conservancy. You can still see the famous parks by day, then switch to a conservancy for the after-dark hours. Our guide to Kenya park fees shows how the daily costs compare.

Night Game Drives in the Masai Mara Conservancies

The Masai Mara conservancies are the most popular place for night game drives in Kenya. They border the reserve and share its wildlife. Camps inside conservancies such as Mara Naboisho, Mara North, Olare Motorogi and Ol Kinyei run night game drives in Kenya's busiest predator country for their own guests.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Inside the main reserve, drives finish at dusk, so the only way to experience the Mara at night is to stay in a conservancy. The trade-off is that you drive into the reserve for big river-crossing days during the migration, which can mean longer drives and an extra daily fee. Our comparison of the Masai Mara reserve and conservancies sets out the pros and cons.

Each conservancy has a different feel. Mara Naboisho Conservancy is known for large lion prides and walking safaris, while Olare Motorogi limits beds tightly to keep sightings uncrowded. Night game drives in Kenya's conservancies all follow the same pattern: a short, slow loop near camp with a guide, a spotter and a filtered light.

What happens on a Mara conservancy night drive?

Most night game drives in Kenya's Mara conservancies leave camp straight after sundowners or after dinner and last around two hours. A spotter sweeps a red or filtered light across the grass, looking for eyeshine. When an animal is found, the light is held off its eyes, and the vehicle keeps its distance so hunts are not disturbed.

Ol Pejeta and Laikipia: Night Game Drives in Kenya’s North

Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Laikipia offers one of the easiest night game drives in Kenya to book. Its 2026 tariff lists a night drive at USD 70 per adult and USD 35 per child (ages 3 to 11), with daily slots from 7pm to 9pm and 9pm to 11pm (checked October 2026).

Photo: Divulge Adventures

According to the Ol Pejeta Conservancy 2026 tariff guide, night drives must be booked at least a day ahead, need a minimum of four people, use shared vehicles and depend on weather and animal welfare. Conservancy entry is a separate USD 110 per non-resident adult per 24 hours. Prices change, so confirm before you travel.

Ol Pejeta is about a 3-4 hour drive north of Nairobi, which makes it an easy add-on to a Samburu or Mount Kenya circuit. Read our Ol Pejeta Conservancy guide for the rhinos, the chimpanzee sanctuary and where to stay, including the Ol Pejeta Safari Cottages.

Laikipia conservancies and the black leopard

Beyond Ol Pejeta, many Laikipia conservancies include night game drives in Kenya's north in their camp rates. This is the region where Kenya's rare black leopard lives, and after-dark drives also turn up striped hyena, aardwolf and porcupine. Our Laikipia Wilderness guide covers the conservancies, the leopard sightings and how to get there.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Our 5 Day Black Leopard and Rhino Photography Safari includes a night game drive at Ewaso Enclave Conservancy in Laikipia, alongside black leopard tracking and a visit to the rhinos of Solio.

What Animals Will You See on a Night Game Drive?

On night game drives in Kenya you see a different cast from daytime safaris: small nocturnal mammals that hide by day, plus big cats and hyenas at their most active. No sighting is guaranteed, but a two-hour drive in a good conservancy usually turns up several species you would never see in daylight.

AnimalHow likelyWhat to look for
Spotted hyenaCommonLoud whooping calls, often moving between kills
LionCommon in the MaraPrides on the move or hunting after dark
LeopardOccasionalEyeshine in trees or along riverbeds
Genet and civetCommonSmall spotted cats moving through scrub
Bushbaby (galago)CommonBright eyeshine high in acacias
SpringhareCommonBounding like a small kangaroo on open plains
Porcupine and white-tailed mongooseFairly commonSlow-moving shapes along tracks
Aardvark and aardwolfRareA prize sighting for any guide

Birds and the night sky

Night game drives in Kenya are also good for owls, including the large Verreaux's eagle-owl, and nightjars that rest on the warm tracks. On clear, moonless nights the stars are spectacular, and many guides stop the vehicle and switch off the light for a few minutes to show you the Southern Cross and the Milky Way.

How Much Do Night Game Drives in Kenya Cost?

Night game drives in Kenya cost about USD 70 per adult at Ol Pejeta (2026 tariff, checked October 2026). In most Mara and Laikipia conservancy camps the drive is included in the full-board camp rate, so the real cost is the higher nightly price of a conservancy stay rather than a separate ticket.

OptionHow it is pricedTip
Ol Pejeta night driveUSD 70 adult / USD 35 child (checked October 2026)Book a day ahead; minimum 4 people
Mara conservancy campUsually included in the full-board rateAsk the camp if it is daily or on request
Laikipia conservancy campOften included in the camp rateConfirm the minimum age for children
KWS national parksNot a standard activityPlan a conservancy night instead

Conservancy camps cost more than reserve lodges because the fees fund landowner leases and conservation, and bed numbers are limited. For a full breakdown of budgets by tier, see our Kenya safari cost guide.

How to Plan Night Game Drives in Kenya

To plan night game drives in Kenya, choose at least one conservancy stay of two nights or more, ask the camp whether night drives run daily, and book any paid drive at least a day ahead. Two nights gives you one spare evening if rain or a full vehicle cancels the first attempt.

Best time of year for night game drives in Kenya

The dry seasons, roughly late June to October and January to February, are the best time for night game drives in Kenya. Grass is shorter, animals gather near water and tracks stay passable. In the long rains of April and May some camps close and drives are more often cancelled because of mud.

Sample itinerary with a night drive

DayWhereHighlight
Day 1-2Ol Pejeta ConservancyRhinos by day, Ol Pejeta night drive on the first evening
Day 3-4SamburuNorthern specials such as reticulated giraffe and Grevy's zebra
Day 5-7Masai Mara conservancyBig cats by day, conservancy night drive, optional walking safari

Pair this with a few nights at the coast or Amboseli if you have more time. Our 7 Day Special Five Ol Pejeta, Meru and Samburu Safari is a good starting point for the northern half of this route.

Insider Tips

  • Pack layers: Open vehicles get cold fast after dark: bring a fleece, a windproof jacket and a hat
  • Skip the flash: Flash and white torches disturb animals; raise your ISO and brace the camera instead
  • Ask for a red filter: Good guides use red or filtered light and keep it off the animal's eyes
  • Go twice: If you stay two nights, book a second drive: sightings vary a lot night to night
  • Insect repellent: Mosquitoes are most active at dusk; cover up and use repellent
  • Check minimum ages: Some camps restrict night drives for young children

Frequently Asked Questions

Are night game drives allowed in the Masai Mara?

Night game drives are not allowed inside the Masai Mara National Reserve, where vehicles must be back in camp or out of the reserve by dusk. They are allowed in the private conservancies that border it, such as Mara Naboisho, Mara North, Olare Motorogi and Ol Kinyei, where camps run them for their own guests.

How much does a night game drive in Kenya cost?

A night game drive in Kenya costs from about USD 70 per adult at Ol Pejeta Conservancy (USD 35 per child, 2026 tariff, checked October 2026). In the Mara and Laikipia conservancies, night drives are usually included in the full-board conservancy camp rate rather than charged separately. Always confirm the current price when booking.

Can you do a night game drive in Kenya's national parks?

Night game drives are not a standard activity in Kenya's national parks. Kenya Wildlife Service asks day visitors to leave by about 6pm unless they are camping inside, and after-dark driving is restricted. A few lodges arrange night activities by special permission, so if a night drive matters to you, plan to stay in a private conservancy.

What animals can you see on a night game drive in Kenya?

On a night game drive in Kenya you can see animals that are rarely seen by day: aardvark, porcupine, genets, civets, bushbabies, springhares, white-tailed mongoose, bat-eared fox and caracal. Lions, hyenas and leopards are also more active after dark, and owls and nightjars are common sightings along the tracks.

Are night game drives safe for children?

Night game drives are generally suitable for older children who can sit quietly for two hours, and Ol Pejeta lists a child rate for ages 3 to 11. Some conservancy camps set minimum ages for night activities, so check with the camp first. Warm layers matter, because open vehicles get cold after dark.

Final Thoughts

Night game drives in Kenya happen in conservancies, not in the Masai Mara National Reserve or as a routine activity in the national parks. Build in two nights at a Mara or Laikipia conservancy, or book the Ol Pejeta night drive a day ahead, and you will see a side of the bush most visitors miss.
